hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-01.question: Since when have private-sector employers with at least 250 employees (as a rule) been required to have an internal reporting channel under the Hinweisgeberschutzgesetz (HinSchG)?

options.a: Since 1 January 2023
options.b: Since 2 July 2023
options.c: Since 17 December 2023
options.d: Not until 1 January 2025

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-01.explanation: The HinSchG entered into force on 2 July 2023; for employers with at least 250 employees (as a rule) the duty to set up an internal reporting channel applied from that date. 17 December 2023 is the date from which the duty also applied to employers with 50-249 employees, not to the larger companies. 1 January 2023 predates the Act's entry into force.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-02.question: A company regularly employs 80 people. From what date did it have to have an internal reporting channel in place?

options.a: From 2 July 2023, the same as all other companies
options.b: Never - companies with under 250 employees are exempt entirely
options.c: From 17 December 2023, because employers with 50-249 employees had a longer transition period
options.d: Only after a case-by-case review by the Bundesamt für Justiz

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-02.explanation: Employers with 50-249 employees (as a rule) had an extended transition period until 17 December 2023, from which date they too had to have an internal reporting channel in place. There is no blanket exemption for smaller companies, and the Bundesamt für Justiz does not conduct a case-by-case review of whether the duty applies.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-03.question: How do employers with fewer than 50 employees fare regarding the duty to set up an internal reporting channel?

options.a: They are always obliged, as soon as they engage in even one activity subject to reporting duties
options.b: As a rule, they are not obliged to set up an internal reporting channel, apart from a few sector-specific special rules
options.c: They must set up the same reporting channel as companies with 250+ employees, just on a later deadline
options.d: They may permanently opt out of the duty simply by filing a written declaration with the Bundesamt für Justiz

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-03.explanation: The core duty to set up an internal reporting channel under §12 HinSchG is tied to the 250- and 50-employee thresholds; businesses with fewer than 50 employees are, as a rule, not covered, although certain regulated sectors (e.g. financial services) may have separate, independent special duties. There is no opt-out via written declaration to the Bundesamt für Justiz - the external reporting channel remains available regardless of any internal company declaration.

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-04.question: How does the internal-reporting-channel duty apply to public-sector employers (e.g. authorities, municipalities)?

options.a: Public-sector employers are entirely exempt, since the HinSchG only applies to the private sector
options.b: Public-sector employers must always set up a reporting channel regardless of size, with no threshold rule at all
options.c: Public bodies are subject to their own rules broadly comparable to the private-sector thresholds, and smaller municipalities may in some cases be grouped together
options.d: Public-sector employers may only have their reporting channel operated directly by the Bundesamt für Justiz

hinweisgeberschutz-geltungsbereich-04.explanation: The HinSchG does not only cover the private sector - it also obliges public-sector employers to set up internal reporting channels, under their own rules broadly similar to the private-sector thresholds, with special provisions for e.g. smaller municipalities. There is no blanket exemption for the public sector, and no requirement that it be run exclusively by the Bundesamt für Justiz - that body operates the external federal reporting channel, not a given authority's internal channel.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-01.question: What requirement does the HinSchG impose on the person(s) who staff the internal reporting channel?

options.a: They must always be a member of the company's executive management
options.b: They must have the necessary expertise and carry out the role independently and free of conflicts of interest
options.c: They must come exclusively from the company's legal department
options.d: They must first be accredited by the Bundesamt für Justiz before they may act

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-01.explanation: Under §§12-13 HinSchG, the employer must set up a competent, independent internal reporting channel; the people entrusted with it need the expertise the task requires and must be independent and free of conflicts of interest. The law does not require the role to be restricted to executive management or the legal department, and there is no accreditation requirement with the Bundesamt für Justiz for internal reporting channels.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-02.question: May a company outsource the operation of its internal reporting channel to an external ombudsperson or law firm?

options.a: No, the reporting channel must always consist of the company's own employees
options.b: Yes, the task can be assigned to an internal unit or outsourced to an external ombudsperson or law firm, as long as independence and expertise are maintained
options.c: Yes, but only if the company has fewer than 50 employees
options.d: No, outsourcing is only permitted with prior case-by-case approval from the Bundesamt für Justiz

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-02.explanation: The HinSchG expressly allows the internal reporting channel to be operated either by an internal unit or delegated to a third party - such as an external ombudsperson or a law firm - as long as the required independence and expertise are maintained. There is no restriction to the company's own employees, no approval requirement from the Bundesamt für Justiz, and no size limit to small companies for this option.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-03.question: Within what deadline must the reporting channel acknowledge receipt of a report to the whistleblower under §17 HinSchG?

options.a: Within 24 hours
options.b: Within 7 days
options.c: Within 30 days
options.d: Within 3 months

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-03.explanation: §17 HinSchG requires the reporting channel to acknowledge receipt of a report within 7 days. The 3-month period does not apply to this acknowledgement but to the later feedback on planned or taken follow-up measures. 24 hours and 30 days are not the deadlines set by the Act for this step.

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-04.question: A manager tells an employee she must report her suspicion internally first - she may only contact the external reporting channel at the Bundesamt für Justiz if the internal channel fails to respond, and disclosing to the press is never protected anyway. What is actually correct?

options.a: Both are correct: internal-before-external is mandatory, and disclosure to the press is never protected
options.b: Whistleblowers can freely choose between the internal and external reporting channel, without first having to try the internal one; disclosure to the public is only protected as a last resort under narrow conditions (e.g. no response from the reporting channels, imminent danger to the public, or risk of retaliation/evidence destruction)
options.c: There is no mandatory order of precedence, but disclosure to the press is always fully protected with no conditions at all
options.d: Internal-before-external is mandatory, whereas disclosure to the press is always protected

hinweisgeberschutz-meldestellen-04.explanation: The HinSchG places the internal and external reporting channel on an equal footing - a person can choose freely, without having to try the internal route first. Disclosure to the public (e.g. the press), by contrast, is protected only as a last resort under narrow, statutorily named conditions, such as no response from the reporting channels, imminent danger to the public interest, or a risk of retaliation or destruction of evidence. Both misconceptions - a forced internal first step and a blanket protected or unprotected view of press disclosure - can in practice deter whistleblowers from choosing the correct channel, which is why this point is considered particularly consequential.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-01.question: Whose identity must the reporting channel treat as confidential, as a rule, under §8 HinSchG?

options.a: Only the whistleblower's identity
options.b: Only the identity of the person the report is directed against
options.c: Both the whistleblower's identity and that of the person implicated or accused in the report
options.d: Nobody's identity - confidentiality is only a non-binding recommendation, not a legal duty

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-01.explanation: §8 HinSchG obliges the reporting channel to keep both the whistleblower's identity and that of the implicated or accused person confidential, subject to narrow, statutorily named exceptions. This is a genuine legal duty, not a mere recommendation, and it is not limited to protecting only one of the two sides.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-02.question: Is the confidentiality duty regarding the whistleblower's identity absolute, with no exceptions at all?

options.a: Yes, the identity may never be disclosed under any circumstances, not even to law enforcement authorities
options.b: No, the Act provides narrowly limited, specifically named exceptions in which disclosure is permitted
options.c: No, any manager may disclose the identity whenever they consider it factually warranted
options.d: Yes, except where the whistleblower has personally requested full anonymity in writing

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-02.explanation: Confidentiality is the rule, but not without exception: the Act names narrowly defined cases in which disclosure is permitted, for example in connection with certain administrative or judicial proceedings. The Act does not grant individual managers a general discretion to disclose - that would undermine the protective purpose of the law.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-03.question: For how long must the reporting channel, as a rule, retain the documentation of a received report before it must be deleted?

options.a: 6 months
options.b: 3 years
options.c: 10 years
options.d: Indefinitely - there is no deletion duty

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-03.explanation: Under §11 HinSchG, documentation of a report must, in essence, be retained for around three years after the procedure concludes and then deleted, unless another legal basis requires or justifies continued storage. Indefinite retention with no deletion duty would run counter to both the data-protection and confidentiality rationale of the Act.

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-04.question: An employee working at the reporting channel casually mentions over lunch to a colleague who submitted a particular report, thinking it is harmless office chat. How should this be assessed?

options.a: Not a problem, as long as the information is not shared in writing or by email
options.b: A breach of the confidentiality duty under §8 HinSchG, which can carry a fine and exposes the whistleblower to real risk
options.c: Not a problem, because the confidentiality duty only applies towards external third parties, not within the company
options.d: Only a problem if the colleague in turn passes the information on further

hinweisgeberschutz-vertraulichkeit-04.explanation: The confidentiality duty under §8 HinSchG applies regardless of the communication medium and also applies within the company - a casual verbal disclosure of the identity is just as much a breach as a written one. Such a breach can carry a fine and exposes the whistleblower to exactly the risk (e.g. retaliation from colleagues or superiors) that the Act is meant to protect against - which is why this misunderstanding is particularly dangerous, regardless of whether the information is spread any further.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-01.question: What does §36(1) HinSchG provide regarding retaliation against whistleblowers?

options.a: Retaliation is allowed as long as it does not become publicly known
options.b: Retaliation is only prohibited for reports made to the external reporting channel, not for internal reports
options.c: Retaliation against persons who have made a report or a disclosure is prohibited
options.d: Retaliation is only prohibited if the reported suspicion later turns out to be accurate

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-01.explanation: §36(1) HinSchG prohibits retaliation against persons who have made a report or disclosure within the meaning of the Act, regardless of whether the report was internal or external and regardless of whether the suspicion is ultimately confirmed. What matters is that there were reasonable grounds to believe the report was accurate at the time it was made, not the later outcome of the investigation.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-02.question: An employee reports a violation and shortly afterwards is not promoted as had otherwise been planned. He suspects a connection. Who must prove whether or not there is a connection to the report?

options.a: The whistleblower must fully prove that the missed promotion was retaliation
options.b: The employer must prove that the missed promotion was NOT based on the report - the burden of proof is reversed
options.c: Neither - such cases are decided exclusively by an arbitration body with no burden-of-proof rule at all
options.d: The whistleblower must prove the report was the cause, but only if he reported externally rather than internally

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-02.explanation: Under §36(2) HinSchG, the burden of proof reverses as soon as a whistleblower suffers a detriment after making a report: the employer must then show and prove that the detriment was NOT based on the report. The widespread assumption that the whistleblower must prove the connection himself is exactly backwards and would effectively gut the protection the Act is meant to provide - which is why this is a particularly dangerous misconception, regardless of whether the report was internal or external.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-03.question: What legal consequence attaches to a retaliatory measure taken despite the prohibition in §36 HinSchG - for example, a dismissal issued in reaction to a report?

options.a: It remains fully valid; the whistleblower can only demand an apology
options.b: It is void or has no legal effect, and the whistleblower can additionally claim damages
options.c: It remains valid as long as the employer gives written reasons for it
options.d: It automatically terminates the entire employment relationship in the whistleblower's favour with double salary

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-03.explanation: Under §37 HinSchG, retaliatory measures within the meaning of §36 HinSchG are void or without legal effect; in addition, the whistleblower can claim damages for the harm suffered. The Act does not provide for a mere duty to apologise or an automatic termination of the contract with double salary, and giving written reasons does not cure an unlawful retaliatory measure.

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-04.question: Which of the following measures, if taken in reaction to a permissible report, could count as a prohibited retaliatory measure within the meaning of §36 HinSchG? (Select all that apply)

options.a: Transferring the whistleblower to a lower-graded position without objective justification
options.b: A routine, performance-based salary adjustment applied equally to all team members regardless of any report
options.c: Bullying or ostracising the whistleblower by managers after the report becomes known
options.d: A compliance training session offered to all employees in the department

hinweisgeberschutz-repressalienschutz-04.explanation: Retaliatory measures within the meaning of §36 HinSchG are detriments connected to a report, e.g. an objectively unjustified transfer to a worse position, or bullying/ostracism by managers. A routine salary adjustment applied equally to everyone and a training offer made to the whole department are neutral measures unrelated to the report and do not constitute retaliation.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-01.question: Up to what amount can a fine be imposed if an employer obstructs a report or subjects a whistleblower to a retaliatory measure?

options.a: Up to €5,000
options.d: No fine is provided for this - only civil damages

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-01.explanation: Obstructing a report and taking retaliatory measures against a whistleblower can both be sanctioned with a fine of up to €50,000. This sanction exists alongside the civil-law damages claim under §37 HinSchG, not instead of it.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-02.question: An obligated employer with 300 employees fails to set up any internal reporting channel at all, despite the statutory duty. What is the maximum fine it must expect for this?

options.a: Up to €5,000
options.b: Up to €50,000, the same as for retaliation
options.d: No fine is threatened, only a non-binding administrative warning

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-02.explanation: Completely failing to set up the legally required internal reporting channel can be sanctioned with a fine of up to €20,000 - a lower maximum than for obstructing a report or for retaliation (each up to €50,000), but still a genuine fine, not a mere administrative warning.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-03.question: An employee at the reporting channel breaches the confidentiality of a whistleblower's identity by disclosing it to third parties without legal grounds. What is the maximum fine provided for this?

options.d: Up to €1,000

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-03.explanation: The unauthorised disclosure of a whistleblower's (or an implicated person's) identity can be sanctioned with a fine of up to €50,000 - the same maximum as for obstructing a report and for retaliation, because the Act treats all of these violations as comparably serious.

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-04.question: Which of the following statements about the fines under the HinSchG is correct?

options.a: There is a single uniform fine range of €50,000 for all violations named in the Act
options.b: The fine amounts differ depending on the violation - among others, up to €20,000 for entirely failing to set up a reporting channel, and up to €50,000 for obstruction, retaliation, or confidentiality breaches
options.c: Fines under the HinSchG can only be imposed on individual employees, never on the company as a whole
options.d: Fines are only provided for in the HinSchG as a non-binding self-commitment by companies, not as a state-enforceable sanction

hinweisgeberschutz-sanktionen-04.explanation: The HinSchG scales the fine ranges according to the severity and type of violation: up to €20,000 for entirely failing to set up a required internal reporting channel, up to €50,000 for obstructing a report, for retaliation, and for confidentiality breaches. These are genuine, state-enforceable administrative-fine (Ordnungswidrigkeiten) sanctions, not a merely voluntary self-commitment, and they can be directed at the company as a whole, not only at individuals.
